paragraphs: We couldn’t take a walk that day. We had wandered through the leafless shrubbery for an hour that morning, but after dinner (Mrs. Reed ate early when there were no guests), the cold winter wind brought dark clouds and a rain so soaking that going outside again was out of the question.

I was glad. I never liked long walks, especially on chilly afternoons. Coming home in the raw twilight, with numb fingers and toes and a heart saddened by Bessie the nurse’s scolding and humbled by knowing I was physically inferior to Eliza, John, and Georgiana Reed, was dreadful to me.

Eliza, John, and Georgiana were now gathered around their mama in the drawing room. She lay reclined on a sofa by the fire, and with her darlings around her (for the moment neither fighting nor crying), she looked perfectly happy. She had excused me from joining the group, saying that “she regretted having to keep me at a distance, but until she heard from Bessie, and could see for herself, that I was making a sincere effort to acquire a more sociable and childlike character, a more attractive and lively manner, something lighter, more open, more natural, as it were, she really had to exclude me from privileges meant only for contented, happy little children.”
“What does Bessie say I’ve done?” I asked.

“Jane, I don’t like quibblers or people who question everything. Besides, there’s something truly disagreeable about a child challenging her elders like that. Sit down somewhere, and until you can speak pleasantly, keep quiet.”

A breakfast room adjoined the drawing room, and I slipped in there. It had a bookcase, and I soon helped myself to a volume, making sure it was one full of pictures. I climbed into the window seat, gathered up my feet, and sat cross-legged like a Turk. Having drawn the red curtain almost shut, I was enclosed in double seclusion.

Folds of scarlet drapery closed off my view on the right. On the left were clear panes of glass, protecting me from the gloomy November day without shutting me off from it. Now and then, as I turned the pages of my book, I studied the look of that winter afternoon. In the distance it was a pale blank of mist and cloud. Nearby was a scene of wet lawn and storm-beaten shrubs, with ceaseless rain being swept wildly along before a long, mournful blast of wind.

I returned to my book, Bewick’s History of British Birds. I didn’t usually care much for the text, and yet there were some introductory pages that, child as I was, I couldn’t pass over as blank. They were the ones about the haunts of seabirds, about “the solitary rocks and headlands” inhabited only by them, and about the coast of Norway, dotted with islands from its southern tip, the Lindesnes, or Naze, to the North Cape:
“Where the Northern Ocean, in vast whirls, Boils round the naked, melancholy isles Of farthest Thule; and the Atlantic surge Pours in among the stormy Hebrides.”

Nor could I ignore the hints of the bleak shores of Lapland, Siberia, Spitsbergen, Novaya Zemlya, Iceland, and Greenland, with “the vast sweep of the Arctic Zone, and those forlorn regions of dreary space—that reservoir of frost and snow, where firm fields of ice, the accumulation of centuries of winters, glazed in Alpine heights above heights, surround the pole and concentrate the multiplied rigors of extreme cold.” Of these death-white realms I formed an idea of my own: shadowy, like all the half-understood notions that drift dimly through children’s minds, but strangely powerful. The words in these introductory pages linked themselves to the illustrations that followed and gave meaning to the rock standing alone in a sea of waves and spray, to the broken boat stranded on a desolate coast, and to the cold, ghastly moon glancing through bars of cloud at a wreck just sinking.

I can’t say what feeling haunted the quite solitary churchyard, with its inscribed headstone, its gate, its two trees, its low horizon, circled by a broken wall, and its newly risen crescent moon, showing the hour of evening.
The two ships becalmed on a sluggish sea, I believed to be ghosts of the ocean.
The fiend pinning down the thief’s pack behind him I passed over quickly. It was an object of terror.
So was the black horned thing sitting apart on a rock, watching a distant crowd gathered around a gallows.

Each picture told a story, often mysterious to my undeveloped understanding and imperfect feelings, yet always profoundly interesting. They were as interesting as the tales Bessie sometimes told on winter evenings, when she happened to be in a good mood, and when, having brought her ironing table to the nursery fire, she let us sit around it. While she pressed Mrs. Reed’s lace frills and crimped the borders of her nightcaps, she fed our eager attention with passages of love and adventure from old fairy tales and ballads, or (as I discovered later) from the pages of Pamela, and Henry, Earl of Moreland.
With Bewick on my knee, I was happy then, at least in my own way. I feared nothing but interruption, and that came too soon. The breakfast room door opened.
“Boo! Madam Mope!” cried the voice of John Reed. Then he paused, because the room seemed to be empty.
“Where the devil is she?” he went on. “Lizzy! Georgy!” (calling to his sisters) “Joan isn’t here. Tell mama she’s run out into the rain, the bad animal!”

“It’s a good thing I drew the curtain,” I thought, and I wished fervently that he wouldn’t discover my hiding place. John Reed wouldn’t have found it himself, because he wasn’t quick, either of sight or of thought. But Eliza just put her head in at the door and said at once:
“She’s in the window seat, of course, Jack.”
And I came out immediately, because I trembled at the idea of being dragged out by Jack.
“What do you want?” I asked, with awkward timidity.
“Say, ‘What do you want, Master Reed?’” was the answer. “I want you to come here.” And sitting down in an armchair, he signaled with a gesture that I was to come and stand in front of him.

John Reed was a schoolboy of fourteen, four years older than I was, because I was only ten. He was large and stout for his age, with a dull, unhealthy skin, thick features in a broad face, and heavy limbs and big hands and feet. He habitually stuffed himself at the table, which made him sickly and gave him dim, bleary eyes and flabby cheeks. He should have been at school by now, but his mama had taken him home for a month or two “on account of his delicate health.” Mr. Miles, the schoolmaster, said he would do very well if he were sent fewer cakes and sweets from home, but the mother’s heart turned away from an opinion so harsh and preferred the more refined idea that John’s sallow look came from overwork and perhaps from missing home.

John had little affection for his mother and sisters and a dislike of me. He bullied and punished me, not two or three times a week, nor once or twice a day, but continually. Every nerve I had was afraid of him, and every bit of flesh on my bones shrank when he came near. There were moments when I was bewildered by the terror he inspired, because I had no appeal against either his threats or his punishments. The servants didn’t want to offend their young master by taking my side against him, and Mrs. Reed was blind and deaf on the subject. She never saw him strike me or heard him abuse me, though he did both now and then in her very presence, more often, however, behind her back.

Used to obeying John, I came up to his chair. He spent about three minutes sticking his tongue out at me as far as he could without hurting the roots. I knew he would hit me soon, and while I dreaded the blow, I thought about how disgusting and ugly the person was who was about to deal it. I wonder if he read that thought in my face, because all at once, without speaking, he struck me suddenly and hard. I staggered, and when I regained my balance, I stepped back a pace or two from his chair.
“That’s for your impudence in answering mama a while ago,” he said, “and for your sneaking way of hiding behind curtains, and for the look in your eyes two minutes ago, you rat!”
Used to John Reed’s abuse, I never thought of replying to it. My concern was how to endure the blow that would certainly follow the insult.
“What were you doing behind the curtain?” he asked.
“I was reading.”
“Show me the book.”
I went back to the window and fetched it.

“You have no business taking our books. You’re a dependent, mama says. You have no money. Your father left you none. You should be begging, not living here with gentlemen’s children like us, eating the same meals we do and wearing clothes at our mama’s expense. Now I’ll teach you to rummage through my bookshelves, because they’re mine. The whole house belongs to me, or will in a few years. Go and stand by the door, out of the way of the mirror and the windows.”

I did so, not realizing at first what he intended. But when I saw him lift the book, balance it, and stand ready to hurl it, I instinctively jumped aside with a cry of alarm. Not quickly enough, however. The book was thrown, it hit me, and I fell, striking my head against the door and cutting it. The cut bled, the pain was sharp, my terror had passed its peak, and other feelings took its place.
“Wicked and cruel boy!” I said. “You’re like a murderer. You’re like a slave driver. You’re like the Roman emperors!”
I had read Goldsmith’s History of Rome and had formed my opinion of Nero, Caligula, and the rest. I had also silently drawn comparisons that I never thought I’d announce out loud like this.
“What! What!” he cried. “Did she say that to me? Did you hear her, Eliza and Georgiana? Just wait till I tell mama! But first—”

He ran headlong at me. I felt him grab my hair and my shoulder. He had come to grips with a desperate creature. I truly saw him as a tyrant, a murderer. I felt a drop or two of blood from my head trickle down my neck and was aware of a stinging pain. These sensations took over from fear for the moment, and I met him in a frenzy. I don’t quite know what I did with my hands, but he called me “Rat! Rat!” and bellowed aloud. Help was near. Eliza and Georgiana had run for Mrs. Reed, who had gone upstairs. She now came on the scene, followed by Bessie and her maid Abbot. We were pulled apart, and I heard the words:
“Goodness! Goodness! What a fury, to fly at Master John!”
“Did anyone ever see such a picture of rage!”
Then Mrs. Reed added:
“Take her away to the red room and lock her in there.” Four hands were immediately laid on me, and I was carried upstairs.
